opening.headline: This explains why AI service images are growing to several gigabytes and take a long time to build, by examining the approach to writing Dockerfiles.
body: When creating AI services in containers, images can grow to several gigabytes, taking minutes just to download. It's also common for dependencies to be reinstalled and the service to be restarted even when only a single line of code has changed. These issues mostly arise from using Dockerfile-based approaches.

This lesson sequentially examines multi-stage builds, using a .dockerignore file to reduce build context, the behavior of layer caching, and the nature of image tags. Finally, it diagnoses a case where model weights are included in the image, causing it to grow larger.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Multi-stage build, .dockerignore, and the role of image tags can be explained.
You can find the causes of image size and reproducibility issues in the Dockerfile.

screens.title: Images are several gigabytes, and builds start from scratch every time.
screens.lead: A team responsible for operating AI service images typically encounters four common symptoms. Selecting any one of these symptoms reveals potential causes.

visual.alt: A diagram showing a list line displaying image sizes in several gigabytes and a timeline indicating that the build steps are being rerun from the beginning.
labels: After modifying one line of code

items.prompt: The image grows up to several gigabytes, taking minutes just to download.
items.answer: It is likely that the image contains files unnecessary for execution. Representative examples include compilers, build tools, the full source code, notebook outputs, and model files. The suspected causes are leftover unnecessary files and build tools.

items.prompt: Changing just one line of code causes the dependency installation step to be re-executed.
items.answer: Docker checks whether each step can be reused from the cache while executing commands in sequence. When an upper step changes, all steps below it are re-executed. The suspected cause is cache invalidation, and the order of commands is the key.

items.prompt: The build tools and compiler are directly included in the operating image.
items.answer: If build-time tools remain in the execution image, it increases the image size and expands the attack surface. This is a signal that build images and operational images have not been distinguished.

items.prompt: The same Dockerfile yields different results today compared to yesterday.
items.answer: Image tags are mutable, allowing publishers to move the same tag to a new image. If the base image tag refers to different content, the same Dockerfile produces different results. The suspect factor is mutable tags.

screens.outro: The question of this class is one: what accelerates image building, and what slows down and makes builds unstable?

screens.title: Preview: Reduced image size experience
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please think about the answer mentally before entering or submitting it.

items.prompt: Have you ever reduced image size before? What did you remove at that time?
items.answer: In many cases, the first thing that stands out is the build tool, package cache, and the entire source repository. Reducing size is more effective by avoiding inclusion from the start than by simply removing existing components. The following screen outlines methods for excluding components initially.

items.prompt: What accounted for the largest proportion among them?
items.answer: In AI services, dependency libraries and model files often account for a significant portion of the total size. To identify which layer contributes the most, it's necessary to first establish the layer-by-layer size of images, developing the habit of checking this information.

items.prompt: When rebuilding the same Dockerfile, at which step did the cache hit?
items.answer: Typically, the upper stage runs in cache, and the lower stage is then re-executed starting from the point where the code has changed. The specific stage from which re-execution begins is determined by the order of Dockerfile commands. Check this point step by step in the second demonstration screen.

screens.outro: Having organized my experience, let's now examine the first strategy, multi-stage build.

screens.title: Multi-stage build: separate build and execution
screens.lead: Select the button to change the state and compare the single-stage Dockerfile and multi-stage Dockerfile alternately.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing the configuration of single-stage images and multi-stage images.

states.label: Before: Single stage
states.body:
Once dependencies are installed and the build process is completed within a single stage, the final image ends up containing the compiler, build tools, and source code. For example, this Dockerfile, which starts with `FROM python:3.12` and installs the required packages before running the build, fits this scenario.

This image is large and takes a long time to download. Since it includes tools that are not needed at runtime, it also increases the attack surface. The documentation explains that in later development stages, images might not require compilers, build systems, or debugging tools.

states.label: After: Multi-stage
states.body:
The Dockerfile commands are divided into multiple stages. In the first stage (e.g., `builder`), dependencies are installed and the build is performed, and in the second stage, the build starts from a slim base and only retrieves the final output as `COPY --from=builder`.

The final image contains only the files necessary to run the application, reducing its size and attack surface. Build stages that are independent of each other can be executed in parallel, enabling efficient builds.

If multiple images share common components, create a reusable stage containing those shared components and stack each image on top of it. Docker builds the common stage only once, making maintenance easier than repeatedly performing the same operations across multiple stages.

screens.outro: Even if you divide the stage, if the build is slow, the reason lies in the cache. Let's examine the layer cache in the next screen.

screens.title: Layer cache and .dockerignore
screens.lead: Follow step by step to see how the cache changes when you fix a single line of code by selecting the right arrow.

visual.alt: Diagram showing cache hit and miss regions within the layers stacked according to command sequence.

steps.title: Docker checks commands in sequence.
steps.body: When building an image, Docker executes the commands listed in the Dockerfile in order. For each command, it checks whether the results from a previous build can be reused, and if possible, it uses the cache. The documentation explains that understanding how caching is invalidated is key to achieving faster builds.

steps.title: When one layer changes, everything below is rebuilt entirely.
steps.body: If a command's result differs from the cache, that layer is invalidated and all layers below it are re-executed. After copying the source code to `COPY . .` and installing dependencies, even a single line change in the code causes the dependency installation to run again every time.

steps.title: Pushes frequently changing things to the back
steps.body: Copy the dependency list file first, then copy the frequently changing source code afterward. This way, even if you modify the code, the dependency layer continues to use the cached version, and only the source copy step needs to be re-executed. Commands with lower change frequency should be placed higher in the hierarchy.

steps.title: Reduces the context using .dockerignore
steps.body: Files not needed for the build are excluded from the build context by listing them in the `.dockerignore` file. It supports exclusion patterns similar to `.gitignore`; `*.md` excludes Markdown files at the context root, while `**/*.md` is used to exclude files down to subfolders. This allows you to prevent unnecessary files from being included in the image without altering the source repository structure.

steps.title: Install only the necessary components.
steps.body: We do not add packages merely because it might be convenient. The documentation provides an example that a text editor is unnecessary for a database image. Removing unnecessary packages reduces complexity, dependencies, file size, and build time.

steps.title: Multiple line factors are sorted.
steps.body: When multiple packages are linked after `RUN apt-get install`, they are sorted alphabetically. This prevents duplicate installations, makes it easier to update the list, and makes it simpler for people reviewing changes to read. Sorting is not a method for caching but rather a maintenance habit to assist with upkeep.

screens.outro: We've addressed the speed issue; now we'll tackle the reproducibility issues of tags and freshness.

screens.title: Image tag pinning and rebuild policy
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare three ways of handling tags and rebuild options.

tabs.label: Variable tag
tabs.body:
Image tags are dynamic. It means that a publisher can move a tag to a new image. If you write `FROM alpine:3.21`, you will receive the latest patched version available at that moment.

The advantage is that you automatically receive new security patches when rebuilding. The disadvantage is that the same Dockerfile from yesterday and today might produce different results. This approach is suitable when latest version is more important than reproducibility.

tabs.label: Digest fixed
tabs.body:
By attaching a digest in the form of `@sha256:` behind a tag, you ensure that exactly the same image is received. Since the digest is a hash of the image content, it remains unaffected if the publisher moves the tag.

Instead, new patches do not arrive automatically. Therefore, it is recommended to use tools like Dependabot to automate updates and use them together when fixing a digest. Fix the digest when reproducibility is required, and leave updates to be managed by the tool.

tabs.label: --pull
tabs.body:
The image is an immutable snapshot. A build captures the base image and libraries exactly as they exist at that moment. Therefore, to maintain security, dependencies must be updated and the image must be rebuilt periodically.

If `docker build --pull -t my-image:my-tag .` is appended with `--pull`, even if a cached version exists locally, the system will verify and download a newer base image. The responsibility of keeping the base image up to date lies with `--pull`.

tabs.label: --no-cache
tabs.body:
`--no-cache` disables the build cache and rebuilds all layers from scratch. It will receive the latest dependencies from package managers such as `apt-get` or `npm`.

However, `--no-cache` does not fetch a new base image. To fetch a new base image, `--pull` is required. Since these options serve different purposes, they can be used together like `docker build --pull --no-cache`.

screens.outro: We have now examined all the concepts; let's apply them to real AI service cases.

screens.title: Explanation: Cases where the model weights have been embedded into the image and have grown larger
screens.lead: The instructor diagnoses and repairs the enlarged AI service image step by step. Please follow along by selecting the right arrow.

visual.alt: Bar chart showing image size decreasing at each improvement stage.

steps.title: Step 1 Diagnosis: Find the Largest Layer
steps.body: The images for this service are several gigabytes in size. Upon checking the image history, the `COPY` layer, which copies the model weights, is the largest. To address the size issue, you must first determine which layer is largest. Before removing the package speculatively, narrow down the root cause using the history.

steps.title: Stage 2: Unnecessary files entered into the context
steps.body: `COPY . .` Copies the entire project folder into an image. It includes all context such as model weights, the `.git` folder, notebook outputs, and document files. The image directly encapsulates these files within layers.

steps.title: Step 3: Exclude using .dockerignore
steps.body: Exclude files not needed for the build from the context by writing patterns such as `.dockerignore`, `.git`, `notebooks/`, and `**/*.md`. The repository structure remains unchanged, but the number of files included in the image is reduced.

steps.title: Step 4: Separate by multi-stage
steps.body: In the first stage, dependencies are installed using the compiler and build tools, and packages (wheels) are created. In the second stage, only the required artifacts are retrieved starting from a slim base using `COPY --from=builder`. The build tools are removed from the final image.

steps.title: Step 5: Weight outside the image
steps.body: We review the approach of loading model weights at runtime rather than embedding them within the image. The image becomes small, containing only code and dependencies, and weights are updated only when the model changes. This example demonstrates that weight copying was the primary reason for increasing image sizes.

steps.title: Step 6: Tag fixation and order organization
steps.body: Fix the base image tag to ensure consistent results between yesterday and today, and place dependency installation before source copying. When only code changes occur, the dependency layer leverages caching, speeding up the build process. A scheduled regular rebuild using `--pull` is also set up for security patches.

screens.outro: I will conclude by summarizing that the cause is divided into two aspects: size and reproducibility.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Small and Reproducible Images
screens.lead: This course content is summarized from three perspectives: scale, speed, and reproducibility.

paragraphs: To reduce size, separate the build stages. Use a multi-stage build to keep the build tools in the builder stage and include only the necessary files for execution in the final image. The context is `.dockerignore`, and the package retains only the essential components.

**Speed** is determined by the layer cache. When one layer changes, all layers below are rebuilt accordingly, so rarely changing commands are placed on top, while frequently changing source copies are placed below.

These three perspectives are interconnected. Reducing the build size shortens the build time, caching improves the speed of repeated builds, and defining tags and rebuild policies allows us to explain whether the same Dockerfile produces the same result.

**Reproducibility** arises from how tags are handled. Since tags are dynamic, they are fixed into digests to ensure consistent results, and are regularly rebuilt using `--pull` for security purposes. `--no-cache` re-executes the build stage, not the base image.

callout.label: Note
callout.text: Containers are beneficial for scalability and reusability when divided to handle only a single concern. However, there is no strict rule requiring only one process; instead, maintaining a clean and modular structure based on judgment is sufficient.

checks.q: The Dockerfile currently copies the entire source first, then installs dependencies. What is the most appropriate single change to make so that dependency installation is only executed when necessary?
options: Append the --no-cache option to the dependency installation command to always install fresh copies.
Move the frequently changing source COPY to behind the dependency installation stage.
Rearranges the list of installed packages in alphabetical order.
Change the base image tag to latest to avoid cache conflicts
checks.explain: If one layer is invalidated, all layers below it are rebuilt. By placing frequent source copies after dependency installation, the cache of dependency layers is preserved.

wrong.0: --no-cache makes all steps run from scratch, which can actually make it slower.
wrong.2: Sorting is intended to make change logs more readable and does not resolve cache invalidation issues.
wrong.3: Variable tags do not relate to caching issues in dependency layers; they only degrade reproducibility.

glossary.def: This approach divides the Dockerfile into multiple stages to include only the artifacts necessary for execution in the final image.
This file contains file patterns to exclude from the build context. It uses a similar syntax to .gitignore.
This is a label pointing to an image version. It is a mutable reference allowing the publisher to move to another image.
This feature allows reusing layers created in previous builds. When an upper layer changes, the layers below it become invalid.
This is a hash of the image content. When appended to a tag, it ensures that the same image is always retrieved.

misconceptions.myth: Since a tag has been specified, the same image is always received.
misconceptions.fact: Tags are mutable, so publishers can move them to different images. To ensure reproducibility, freeze them using a digest, and automate updates using tools like Dependabot.

misconceptions.myth: --no-cache means the base image will be updated to the latest version.
misconceptions.fact: --no-cache is an option that re-executes all stages without caching, but it does not retrieve a new base image. The base image retrieval is handled by --pull, and both options can be used together.

misconceptions.myth: It's simpler to put all processes into a single container.
misconceptions.fact: Dividing containers so that each handles only one concern makes horizontal scaling and reuse easier. The rule of having one process is not strict, so modularization can be done based on judgment.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The image separates the build stage, thereby reducing the size.
Reduce build time with caching and a .dockerignore file.
Tags are mutable, so they are used together with fixed and periodic rebuilds.
Unnecessary packages and files are not included in the image.
